I want to write about attention, the way it narrows and expands, and how the act of writing is really an act of choosing what to notice. But perhaps that's too meta. Let me instead write about a morning walk.

This morning I walked before the sun had fully cleared the rooftops. The air had that particular clarity that only comes after rain, when the dust has been beaten down and the smells of wet asphalt and earth rise up. I saw a snail making its way across the sidewalk, leaving a silver trail. It was moving with impossible slowness, and yet there was something heroic in it—this tiny creature carrying its home, inching toward a patch of grass. I stopped and watched for a minute. A woman with a dog passed, and the dog strained toward the snail, but the woman pulled it away, not noticing the tiny life at her feet. I wondered how many small dramas I miss every day.

There is a particular quality to early morning light. It has no heat yet, only illumination. It makes the world look new, as if the night has rinsed away the previous day's residue. I passed a house with a garden overgrown with roses. The roses were heavy with rainwater, their heads bowed. Some petals had fallen and lay scattered on the path like pink confetti. I thought about how beauty often comes from things that are temporary. A rose in full bloom is already beginning to fade. Maybe that's why we find it beautiful.

I kept walking. The street was quiet except for the occasional car. I heard a bird—a blackbird, I think—singing from a telephone wire. Its song was complex, full of trills and pauses. I tried to imitate it, but my whistle was pitiful. The bird didn't seem to mind. I thought about how animals communicate in ways we can't understand, and how much of the world is happening in frequencies and languages beyond our perception. There are bats clicking above us at dusk, whales singing across oceans, trees sending chemical signals through fungal networks underground. The world is full of conversations we cannot hear.

Writing about a walk feels indulgent. But maybe that's the point. We are so often told to be productive, to optimize, to hurry. But there is value in slowness. The snail taught me that. It wasn't wasting time; it was simply moving at the pace its body required. Perhaps we could learn to move at the pace our attention requires, rather than the pace the world demands.

I've been thinking about silence. Real silence is rare now. Even in the early morning, there is the hum of a distant highway, the buzz of a transformer, the faint whine of an airplane. I read once that silence is not the absence of sound but the absence of human-made sound. That seems right. The rustle of leaves, the drip of water from a gutter, the call of a bird—these are not noise. They are the world breathing. When I write, I often seek silence, but what I really need is to hear the world without interruption. I need to hear my own thoughts.

There is a strange loneliness in writing. You sit alone with your thoughts and try to arrange them into something coherent. Sometimes the thoughts resist. They scatter like startled birds. Other times they flow easily, and you feel as if you are merely taking dictation from some deeper part of yourself. I don't understand where ideas come from. They seem to emerge from a dark pool, rising to the surface when you least expect them. Often the best ideas come when you are not trying—in the shower, on a walk, in the moment between sleep and waking. Maybe that's why walking is so important for writers. It gives the mind permission to wander.

I passed a small park. The playground was empty, the swings hanging still. A puddle had formed under the slide, and a sparrow was taking a bath in it, fluffing its feathers and shaking off water. I smiled. There is something comical about birds bathing. They seem so earnest. I thought about how animals don't worry about how they look. They simply do what they need to do. The sparrow didn't care that I was watching. It was fully absorbed in its bath. That kind of absorption is rare in humans. We are always aware of being watched, of how we appear. Even when alone, we carry an internal audience.

The walk continued. I smelled coffee from a house where someone was starting their day. I thought about all the lives happening behind closed doors. Each house contained stories—breakfasts being made, arguments, laughter, tears. We pass by these houses and know nothing of what happens inside. It's a strange thing about cities: we live so close together, yet we are strangers. In a village, everyone knows your business. In a city, you can be anonymous. Both have their comfort and their cost.

I turned a corner and saw a cat sitting on a wall, watching me with yellow eyes. It didn't move as I passed, just followed me with its gaze. Cats seem to exist in a different time signature. They are patient in a way humans rarely are. I thought about how much of our lives are spent waiting—for a bus, for a response, for the weekend. But waiting implies that the present moment is not enough. The cat seemed to have no such problem. It was entirely present, entirely itself.

The sun was higher now, and the light had changed from silver to gold. The shadows were shorter. The city was waking up. More cars, more people. A jogger passed me, breathing hard. A delivery van double-parked. The quiet was receding. I felt a small pang of loss. The early morning is a secret that few people share. By midday, the world becomes loud and fast, and the small things—the snail, the bathing sparrow, the bowed roses—become invisible again.

I walked home, carrying the quiet with me.
